teaser: Two broke friends, one riverside café, and the summer that taught painters how to do water.
review_notes:
'Frogs' as a nickname for the easygoing young women who came to La Grenouillère: standard explanation.
The islet's nickname 'Camembert' (also 'the flowerpot').
Sign on the floating café reads as boat rental (location de canots); only part of the lettering is legible in the image.
Renoir's companion picture is in the Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.
Monet's 'bad sketches' remark is from a letter to Bazille, September 1869; Renoir bringing bread from his parents' table is from Renoir's recollections.
Larger Grenouillère by Monet formerly in a Berlin collection, lost in World War II and known from a photograph.
John Goffe Rand's collapsible paint tube, 1841.

lesson.text: How would you paint something that never keeps the same shape for two seconds? A river on a sunny day is a mess of moving glints, and no brush is fast enough to copy them. Until the 1860s most painters solved this by smoothing water into a calm mirror. Monet, at 28, tried something else.

In the summer of 1869 he set up his easel on the bank of the Seine, a short train ride west of Paris, facing a popular bathing spot. His friend Pierre-Auguste Renoir set up right beside him. The two painted the same view, on the same days, almost elbow to elbow.
La Grenouillère means “the frog pond.” The frogs in question were not animals. It was a cheeky nickname for the carefree young women who came out from Paris to swim, flirt and dance there.

The place was simple. A floating café was moored to the bank, on the right. Narrow gangplanks led from it to a tiny round island with one tree, which regulars nicknamed “the Camembert” after the cheese. You could rent a rowboat, order a drink, or just jump in the river.
Some visitors are already in the water. Can you find the swimmers?

spots.title: The bathers
spots.text: To the left of the islet, a few pink and dark blobs bob at the surface: heads and shoulders of people standing in the shallows. One raises an arm toward the island.

lesson.text: A head is one touch of pink. A body is one stroke of black. Monet had no time for more, and he did not want more. He was after the overall impression of a noisy afternoon, the thing you take in before you notice any single person. The same shorthand is what lets him tackle the river.

lesson.title: Three kinds of water
lesson.text: Start near your feet and move back toward the far bank.

spots.title: Up close
spots.text: Wide slabs of black-green, olive, white and sky blue, each laid down once and left alone. Dark means reflected trees, light means reflected sky. Nothing is blended.

spots.title: Middle distance
spots.text: Near the gangplank the strokes get shorter and closer together. The ripples seem smaller because they are farther away.

spots.title: Far away
spots.text: By the opposite bank the water is thin streaks of bright blue and white. Shrinking the brushstroke is how Monet makes the river stretch back.

lesson.text: Monet stopped drawing water and started building it from separate patches of light and dark color. That broken touch became the signature of Impressionism.

Working this fast outdoors depended on a small invention: the squeezable metal paint tube, patented in 1841 by the American painter John Goffe Rand. Before it, oil paint was kept in pig bladders that dried out and burst.
The scene can look like a snapshot, grabbed at random. It is not. Under the sparkle there is a firm frame that sends your eye to one place.
Three lines meet at the little island.

lines.label: The left gangplank
lines.text: A dark plank on stilts runs in from the left edge and delivers you to the islet.

lines.label: The right gangplank
lines.text: A second walkway comes from the floating café. People are crossing it in single file.

lines.label: Tree and reflection
lines.text: The trunk drops from the top of the canvas to the islet, and its dark reflection carries the line on down through the water.

lesson.text: So the islet is a hub, with the tree as its axle. Renoir, standing beside Monet, made a different choice. His version, now in Stockholm, moves in on the people: their dresses, their chatter, a dog. Monet stays back and gives more than half his canvas to the river. One friend was painting a party, the other was painting light.
Monet painted a larger view of La Grenouillère as well. It belonged to a Berlin collection, disappeared during World War II and is known today only from a photograph.

Neither of them thought these pictures were finished works. Monet was so poor that summer that Renoir carried bread to him from his own parents' table. In a letter Monet called his Grenouillère canvases “bad sketches” and dreamed of a big, polished version for the Salon, the official Paris exhibition. Here is what a bad sketch contains.

spots.title: The café sign
spots.text: Capital letters run along the railing of the floating café. The legible part spells “canot,” French for a rowboat: this is where you rented one.

spots.title: Woman in blue
spots.text: A lone figure in a dark blue dress and hat steps onto the gangplank, seen from behind. She is five or six strokes of paint.

spots.title: The crowd
spots.text: Men in dark jackets, women in full skirts, a seated figure in blue. City clothes mingle with swimsuits on a platform a few steps wide.

spots.title: Rental boats
spots.text: Moored rowboats nose in from the corner. Their hulls, cut off by the frame, put you right at the water's edge, as if you were about to climb in.

spots.title: The far bank
spots.text: A wall of trees in yellow-green fills the background, lit by sun. Monet scrubs it in loosely so it stays behind the action.

spots.title: More boats
spots.text: Long slim boats with red-brown trim are tied below the café. Their diagonals point back toward the center.

lesson.text: The grand Salon version never happened. Five years later, in 1874, Monet and Renoir helped organize an independent exhibition, and a critic mocked the group as “Impressionists.” By then the quick sketch from the frog pond was no longer a step toward a painting. It was the painting.

quiz.question: Who painted the same view right beside Monet in 1869?
quiz.explanation: Renoir and Monet worked side by side at La Grenouillère.

quiz.question: How does Monet make the river appear to stretch into the distance?
options: His brushstrokes get smaller farther away
He adds fog over the far bank
He draws lines converging on a vanishing point
quiz.explanation: Wide slabs up close shrink to thin streaks near the far bank.

quiz.question: What was “the Camembert”?
options: A local cheese sold to bathers
The small round island with a tree
quiz.explanation: Regulars nicknamed the round islet after the cheese.

quiz.question: What did Monet call his Grenouillère canvases in a letter?
quiz.explanation: He saw them as preparation for a large Salon painting that never came.

quiz.question: Which invention made fast outdoor oil painting practical?
quiz.explanation: The squeezable tube, patented in 1841, kept paint fresh and portable.

quiz.question: How does Renoir's version differ from Monet's?
options: It shows the scene at night
It moves in closer on the people
quiz.explanation: Renoir focuses on the crowd, Monet on the water and light.

facts.text: La Grenouillère was named after the many frogs living in the river.
facts.explanation: “Frogs” was a nickname for the carefree young women who gathered there.

facts.text: Monet gives more than half of the canvas to the river.
facts.explanation: He stays back from the crowd and lets the water dominate.

facts.text: Monet went on to paint a large, polished version for the Salon.
facts.explanation: The Salon picture never happened; the sketch itself became the finished work.
